title.en: Poems: How to Tell Wild Animals & The Ball Poem
Playful jungle jokes vs learning to let go

text.en: Unit 3 pairs two poems with very different moods: Carolyn Wells jokes about ridiculous ways to spot fierce beasts, while John Berryman watches a boy quietly learn his first real lesson about loss.

In How to Tell Wild Animals, Carolyn Wells offers mock-helpful instructions for identifying wild creatures in Eastern jungles—if you meet them alive!
She says you can tell the Asian Lion by its deadly roar, the Bengal Tiger because he eats you, the Leopard because he keeps leaping ('lep and lep') with peppered spots, and the Bear by its suffocating hug.
She adds witty contrasts for crocodiles (weeping while swallowing prey) vs hyenas (smiling merrily), plus the chameleon disguised invisibly on a branch. Notice playful 'poetic licence' spelling ('lep') and light humour.
In The Ball Poem, John Berryman slows down to observe a young boy whose ball bounces happily down the street and drops straight into deep harbour water.
The speaker intentionally refrains from offering a dime to buy another ball because 'money is external': cash can buy a new ball, not the lost childhood memories tied to that specific ball.
Standing rigid and trembling, the boy discovers what Berryman calls 'the epistemology of loss'—knowing what it means to lose something dear and still stand up bravely.

caption.en: Trace imagery, tone and central idea

text.en: Unit 3 brings together two wonderfully different poems: How to Tell Wild Animals by Carolyn Wells and The Ball Poem by John Berryman.
In How to Tell Wild Animals, Carolyn Wells pretends to write a field guide for spotting wild beasts, using dry humour throughout.
If a large tawny beast roars so loudly you nearly faint, she jokes you have met the Asian Lion.
If a noble black-and-yellow creature calmly greets you only to eat you, that is the Bengal Tiger.

board.text: Bengal Tiger -> black stripes on yellow

text.en: For the Leopard, she uses poetic licence and spells leap as 'lep', joking that he will only keep 'lepping' again and again.
The Bear gives a tight embrace, and she playfully separates the Crocodile's false tears from the Hyena's cheerful smile.

board.text: Bear hug; hyena smile vs croc tears

text.en: Finally, if a tree looks completely empty yet holds a lizard without ears or wings, a hidden chameleon is there.
Now switch tone completely to John Berryman's The Ball Poem, where a boy loses his favourite ball.

board.text: The Ball Poem: losing a treasure

text.en: The ball bounces cheerfully down the street and plunges into the dark water of the harbour out of reach.
An observer watches the boy freeze, shake with grief, and stare down at the water where his young days went.
Someone could easily hand the boy a coin for another ball, yet the poet calls that 'worthless' because no replacement matches the original.
Why? Berryman writes that money is external: it pays for new objects, never for emotional attachment or time.
Through this small loss, the boy senses his first responsibility and learns the epistemology of loss—the true meaning of losing something.
Growing up means accepting that possessions, moments, and treasures vanish in a world of possessions, yet learning how to stand back up.

board.text: Learning to stand up after loss

problem.en: Contrast the poetic technique in 'He'll only lep and lep again' with 'money is external' in Unit 3.

text.en: Wells alters spelling ('lep') to keep rhyme and playful comic rhythm.

why.en: Poetic licence intentionally bends standard spelling for humorous effect.

text.en: Berryman states 'money is external' to separate price from emotional value.

why.en: A bought replacement cannot erase the grief of losing an irreplaceable memory.

text.en: Both poems teach clearly: one through absurd exaggeration, the other through quiet reflection.

why.en: Poets choose tone to fit purpose: farce vs coming-of-age depth.

prompt.en: Why does the poet in The Ball Poem refuse to intrude or buy the boy a new ball, and what makes How to Tell Wild Animals funny?

requiredIdeas.en: Wells creates humour by making deadly attacks sound like casual identification clues
Berryman avoids buying a new ball so the boy learns responsibility and handles real loss
Money is external and cannot buy back cherished childhood memories

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the boy cries only because his parents could not afford another dime

points.en: How to Tell Wild Animals uses humorous exaggeration, irony, and poetic licence ('lep') to describe jungle animals.
Distinguishing hyenas (smiles) from crocodiles (tears) and spotting camouflaged chameleons shows playful observation.
In The Ball Poem, losing a ball in a harbour teaches a boy his first sense of responsibility.
'Money is external' highlights that emotional loss cannot simply be bought away; resilience grows from accepting loss.
